subject: Databricks · : Describe a production ML or GenAI system where you did model-level work (training, fine-tuning, optimization, or evaluation) on a transformer-based model (GPT, Llama, Claude, Mistral, Gemma, or similar).
detail: Drafted from your resume and used on the form: "I don’t want to overstate this: my documented transformer model-level work has been evaluation and interpretability research, not a production rollout. In Columbia AI Alignment Club, I worked on Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B: implementing activation hooks across 28 transformer layers, linear probes, steering interventions, randomized and sham controls, grouped-bootstrap controls, and response/token-level evaluations to test whether observed logit shifts reflected reliable hallucination or refusal behavior. Separately, I have deployment-facing experience from a real-time robotics system, where I optimized inference with ONNX Runtime, quantization, asynchronous video pipelines, and integrated a locally hosted language model through Ollama into the robot control workflow. For Databricks AI FDE, I would bring the evaluation rigor from the Qwen work together with practical inference and systems integration experience.". subject: Databricks · : Describe a time you worked directly with an external enterprise customer on an ML/AI problem.
detail: Drafted from your resume and used on the form: "I don’t want to overstate this: I have not yet owned a direct external enterprise customer engagement on an ML/AI problem. The closest analogue is my applied ML work at Arborphy AI, where I worked through an ambiguous domain problem end to end: plant identification and botanical reasoning. I designed and evaluated vision/biological embedding architectures, built disjoint benchmarks for species identification and retrieval, created a human-review set, and developed a multi-agent botanical reasoning prototype with knowledge-graph evidence aggregation. At Columbia, I also made research code usable for non-ML wet-lab researchers through packaging, documentation, and step-by-step guides. That is the customer-facing muscle I would bring to Databricks, while being clear that enterprise client ownership would be a growth area.". subject: Glean · Machine Learning Engineer, Assistant Quality: What AI tools are you currently using today and how are you using them?
detail: Drafted from your resume and used on the form: "Today, in my current Research Engineer Intern role at Arborphy AI, I’m using EfficientNet, BioCLIP, and DINOv3 to study plant-identification models and representation quality. I use frozen linear probes, clustering, nearest-neighbor retrieval, local PCA rotations, and centroid shrinkage to understand whether representations capture species identity, organ morphology, or photographic-scale confounding. I’m also building evaluation loops: individual- and species-disjoint benchmarks for species identification, organ classification, and cross-species retrieval, plus human-review sets for model errors. On the agent side, I’ve built a multi-agent botanical reasoning prototype with autonomous tool generation, visual-analysis agents, constrained planning, per-step information-gain evaluation, and knowledge-graph evidence aggregation. That maps closely to assistant quality work: retrieval, grounding, evaluation, and iterative improvement.". To change it: jh answer answer:draft:abf0cbe503 "<your text>"

subject: Artera · Machine Learning Scientist, Computational Pathology: Tell us about a self-supervised or foundation model you have worked with, whether trained from scratch, pretrained, or adapted to a downstream task. What did you do with it, and how did you evaluate whether it worked well for your use case?
detail: Drafted from your resume and used on the form: "At Arborphy AI, I worked with pretrained BioCLIP and DINOv3 representations for plant identification, treating them as foundation-model features rather than assuming they would transfer cleanly. I designed an EfficientNet–BioCLIP dual-encoder with bidirectional spatial cross-attention, auxiliary organ supervision, and BioCLIP-anchored gated residuals to test whether local visual features and BioCLIP semantics were complementary. I evaluated this with controlled fusion experiments: single encoders, concatenation, and uni- versus bidirectional attention; individual-disjoint, species-disjoint, multi-seed, and grouped held-out benchmarks; frozen linear probes; clustering; nearest-neighbor retrieval; and human review of hard cases. The main result was useful but humbling: fusion macro-F1 improved across iterations from 0.808 to 0.832, but under stricter evaluations I found no reliable species-recognition advantage over BioCLIP alone. That kind of evaluation discipline is what I would bring to Artera’s pathology foundation-model work.". To change it: jh answer answer:draft:e560fd89af "<your text>"

subject: Artera · Machine Learning Scientist, Computational Pathology: Describe a project where your model did not generalize as well as expected across datasets, sites, devices, populations, or other conditions. How did you investigate the problem, and what did you try to improve robustness?
detail: Drafted from your resume and used on the form: "In my current Arborphy AI work on plant identification, I expected an EfficientNet–BioCLIP fusion model to generalize better than BioCLIP alone, but grouped held-out and individual-disjoint evaluations showed no reliable species-recognition advantage. I treated that as a domain-shift question rather than just a tuning problem. I compared single encoders, concatenation, and uni- versus bidirectional cross-attention, then used frozen probes, clustering, nearest-neighbor retrieval, local PCA rotations, and centroid shrinkage to separate species signal from organ morphology and photographic-scale confounding. To improve robustness, I tried auxiliary organ supervision, BioCLIP-anchored gated residuals, individual- and species-disjoint benchmarks, and cross-model error review. That experience maps closely to Artera’s need for pathology models that hold up on messy real-world data.". To change it: jh answer answer:draft:7762bc1ea5 "<your text>"

subject: Artera · Machine Learning Scientist, Computational Pathology: Tell us about a machine-learning project where you had to understand or explain what the model was learning. What methods did you use, and what did you learn from them?
detail: Drafted from your resume and used on the form: "At Arborphy, I worked on a plant-identification model where the main question was not just whether fusion improved accuracy, but what each representation was actually encoding. I compared BioCLIP, DINOv3, and EfficientNet features using frozen linear probes, multi-seed clustering, nearest-neighbor retrieval, local PCA rotations, centroid shrinkage, and cross-model error review. I also ran controlled fusion experiments across single encoders, concatenation, and uni- versus bidirectional cross-attention, with individual-disjoint, multi-seed, and grouped held-out evaluation. The key lesson was that model behavior was partly semantic and partly geometric: DINOv3 carried strong organ-morphology signal, while BioCLIP remained the most reliable for species recognition, and added fusion did not produce a dependable species-recognition gain. That changed how I evaluated “better” architectures: interpretability and robust held-out behavior mattered more than architecture complexity.". To change it: jh answer answer:draft:43ec6314f1 "<your text>"

subject: Artera · Machine Learning Scientist, Computational Pathology: Describe a clinical, biological, or other real-world problem you helped translate into a machine-learning problem. How did you define the prediction target and decide how to evaluate the model?
detail: Drafted from your resume and used on the form: "At Arborphy AI, I worked on translating botanical identification into a supervised representation-learning problem: given plant images, predict species identity while separating signal from organ morphology and photographic-scale confounding. I defined the main target as species identification, with auxiliary organ classification to test whether leaf/flower/fruit cues were helping or causing negative transfer. Because the real risk was a model that memorized individuals or scales rather than biological identity, I emphasized individual-disjoint, species-disjoint, multi-seed, and grouped held-out evaluation, plus cross-species retrieval and human review of hard cases. That is the same kind of rigor I would bring to Artera’s setting: defining clinically meaningful targets from slides and clinical data, then testing whether performance holds under realistic distribution shifts.". detail: Drafted from your resume and used on the form: "Today, in my current Research Engineer Intern role at Arborphy AI, I’m using EfficientNet, BioCLIP, and DINOv3 to study plant-identification models and representation quality. subject: Perplexity · Member of Technical Staff, AI Products (Early Career - Industry): How do you use AI in your day-to-day work? What are some of the underappreciated benefits and/or pain points of your favorite AI tools?
detail: Drafted from your resume and used on the form: "In my current research engineering work, I use AI as an experimental collaborator and as a system component rather than as a black-box answer machine. At Arborphy, that means comparing visual encoders like BioCLIP, DINOv3, and EfficientNet, building a multi-agent botanical reasoning prototype with tool generation and evidence aggregation, and using reproducible evals to decide what actually improves recognition. My favorite tools are local and inspectable ones: Ollama for embedding a language model into a robot workflow, and Hugging Face/TransformerLens-style workflows for inspecting model behavior. The pain point is that models can look persuasive while adding no measurable value: I have seen fusion fail to beat BioCLIP alone, and hallucination-circuit work break down because behavior was unstable and first-token evidence was too weak.". Dishonesty includes acts involving want of integrity, lack of probity, or a disposition to distort, cheat, or act deceitfully or fraudulently, and may include crimes which federal, state, or local laws define as dishonest such as robbery, embezzlement, forgery, perjury, tax evasion, and shoplifting. "Breach of trust" means a wrongful act, use, misappropriation, or omission with respect to any property or funds committed to a person in a fiduciary or official capacity, or the misuse of one's official or fiduciary position to engage in a wrongful act, use, misappropriation, or omission. For purposes of this Application, "dishonesty" means directly or indirectly to cheat or defraud, to cheat or defraud for monetary gain or its equivalent, or to wrongfully take property belonging to another in violation of any criminal statute. Dishonesty includes acts involving want of integrity, lack of probity, or a disposition to distort, cheat, or act deceitfully or fraudulently, and may include crimes which federal, state, or local laws define as dishonest such as robbery, embezzlement, forgery, perjury, tax evasion, and shoplifting.
